20649-oomphel-in-the-sky:
H. Beam Piper's Oomphel in the Sky is a science fiction story set on a colony world far from Earth. It opens with a communication screen snapping on. Harry Walsh, the news editor, looks out from his office in Bluelake, halfway across the continent, and wants to know how things are going.

The man he calls is deep in trouble with the planet's native peoples. Their word oomphel names the strange sky craft and goods they cannot explain. Piper, famous for his future histories, builds the tale on language, trade, and the clash of two worlds' ideas.
20719-under-the-country-sky:
Grace S. Richmond set her novel Under the Country Sky in a country town, among the people her heroine serves and loves. Richmond wrote warm stories of doctors, ministers, and their families in small places. Her heroine's patience with her neighbors is tested on every page.

She loved them all, the narrator explains, so it would go hard with her if she had to hate them. Love turned to hate is such a bitter product. But she had never found it so hard to be patient with them as now. Under that strain, the novel tests what small-town kindness costs the one who gives it.
21568-sweet-their-blood-and-sticky:
Albert R. Teichner's tale Sweet Their Blood and Sticky ran in Worlds of If in November 1961. A vast machine, hundreds of feet long, stands working alone in a desert. It can run on a thimbleful of earth or water, drawing all it needs from the land.

With its packing gear broken, the machine pours out a stream of pink-striped taffy. Once a whole desert of such devices fed a needful human race. Now the makers are gone, and something not human inherits the earth. Teichner builds a chill, strange tale from candy, dust, and four dimensions.
boy-scouts-in-an-airship-or-the-warning-: Ralphson's Boy Scouts take to the air in this early aviation adventure, where a warning from the sky sets them on a daring mission. Part of the popular series that taught scout virtues through thrills. Pure 1910s boy's adventure, with the new wonder of flight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kentucky: This 1913 reference article on Kentucky — the bluegrass missions. Frank Tracy unfolds their rugged tale. The missionaries braved the frontier wilds. The missions' foothold was dearly won. The hills knew their zeal. Their 19th-century missions are famed. Their frontier chapels are famed.
curiosities-of-the-sky: Popular science writer Garrett Serviss tours the wonders of the heavens — strange stars, comets, eclipses, and the mysteries astronomers were just beginning to solve. Written for curious readers with no telescope, his clear, enthusiastic prose makes the universe feel close and marvelous. A delightful classic of popular astronomy.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NSRP-BereaKY_NS: A fragment of a news article covers a rally of the National States Rights Party in Berea, Kentucky. The rally was marked by violence. The article blames the violence on 'outside agitators,' a phrase officials used often in those years. The party was a segregationist organization, and Berea was a small college town. The publication that carried the article is not identified, and the fragment does not preserve its date or its full account.
myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-volume:
Charles M. Skinner rides west along the Rocky Range in this volume. A phantom train on Marshall Pass opens the contents. Lost souls' rivers and riders of the desert follow. A Yellowstone tragedy and a Santa Fe flood raise the peril.

Over the Divide tells of men still hunting El Dorado. Gold in California and Colorado kept that old dream alive. Miners braved hunger, sickness, and death for treasure caves. Navajo tales and a goddess of salt add Native depth. Skinner's West is vast and haunted, where tall tales grow as big as the peaks themselves.
podcast-dannyjones-xXq5o5rW_kY:
Breath coach Will Grant teaches how to fix the body using breath in episode 50 of the KONCRETE podcast with Danny Jones. Grant argues that most people breathe badly and pay for it in stress, pain, and poor sleep. His fix costs nothing and starts with the next inhale.

Grant explains simple breathing patterns and the body systems they affect. He shows how breath can calm nerves, steady the heart, and aid recovery after hard training. Jones tries the methods and asks how to build them into a daily routine. Breathless and curious listeners alike get air treated as real medicine.
podcast-joerogan-5jKEYKrA4kY:
Rogan reacts, in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, to the Biden administration delaying the release of JFK assassination files. By law, the records were due to open in full, and each delay has fed public doubt about what the files hold.

The talk asks why, six decades on, agencies still fight to keep pages sealed. Rogan weighs the official reasons against the suspicion that delay itself is the message. He places the fight in a longer story of government secrecy. For listeners drawn to the Kennedy case, the segment captures the mood of the disclosure fight as it stood then.
podcast-joerogan-uFiR3nVtYKY:
Music producer Rick Rubin sits with Joe Rogan for episode 1881 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Rubin co-founded Def Jam and produced landmark records across rap, rock, and country. He is famous for stripping songs down to what matters and for his calm, zen-like style.

Rubin talks about creativity as a way of paying attention rather than forcing results. He shares how he helps artists trust their taste and cut away the rest. Rogan asks about fame, failure, and making art that lasts. Makers of any kind get a quiet master class in doing less, but better.
the-adventures-of-prickly-porky: Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Adventures of Prickly Porky for his Bedtime Story-Books, with art by Harrison Cady, printed at Boston by Little, Brown, and Company in 1916. Chapters listed open with Happy Jack Squirrel's find and a stranger from the North, then Prickly Porky making friends, Peter Rabbit's startling news, Jimmy Skunk's call, and Reddy Fox in misery.
the-rise-of-david-levinsky: Abraham Cahan is named as author on the edition header. The header gives the title of his novel. It gives a September 2001 release date. A later update followed in March 2009. Only that edition header is present on these pages. Its general notices appear with it. No part of the novel itself appears here. Nothing about David's rise can be told from these pages alone.
the-young-trailers-a-story-of-early-kent: Joseph A. Altsheler's The Young Trailers, copyrighted in 1907, is shown here through its dedication and contents. Altsheler dedicates the Kentucky story to Sydney, a young Kentuckian. Twelve chapters lead into the unknown wilderness. A haunted forest, giant bones, and a wild turkey's gobble appear. The escape and the primitive man close the list shown. The story chapters themselves do not appear in the pages present in this record.
two-little-knights-of-kentucky:
Two Little Knights of Kentucky opens its contents with Two Tramps and a Bear, then a valentine party, a fire, and Jonesy's benefit. A dedication names nine children of the author's circle. No author is named on the pages shown.

Chapter one sets the coldest Saint Valentine's eve Kentucky had known in twenty years. Snow in Lloydsborough Valley shows every rabbit track, and an ice-cutter's wagon creaks up from a pond. Inside the depot waiting-room, a red-hot stove cannot clear the frost from the window-panes. Two boys run up the track with skates in hand, half an hour before the five o'clock train. The knights' adventures begin in that frozen station.
watchers-of-the-sky:
Alfred Noyes wrote Watchers of the Sky as the first volume of The Torch-Bearers, a trilogy in verse on the story of scientific discovery. His prefatory note calls the volume complete in itself. It finds an epic unity in that story: a single torch of purpose and endeavor, passed from hand to hand through the centuries. His poem treats the great moments of the work. After long labor, the pioneers saw their gathered facts fall into a significant order.

Those moments, Noyes says, hold intense human interest. They belong to the creative imagination of poetry. He does not try to cover the whole field, or to build a new system of science in verse. The prologue pictures a night among the stars, when the new hundred-inch telescope was first tried.
